beats.text: Make the first move. It's math!
Let's simulate it. Ten people on each side. Everyone secretly ranks everyone. One side asks. The other side holds on to the best offer so far.
Round after round, until everyone is matched.
Now we check: how happy is each side with their match? Here's the result.
The askers got their number two on average. The ones who waited: number five!
Swap the sides, and it flips. The math is proven: in this model, asking never makes you worse off.
Real dating is messier, of course. But the lesson holds: send the first message.

ask: SEND THE FIRST MESSAGE. THEN SAVE THIS.
sources: Gale & Shapley (1962), College admissions and the stability of marriage, American Mathematical Monthly 69(1), 9–15 – deferred acceptance: the proposing side receives its best partner among all stable matchings; the receiving side its worst.
Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences 2012: Alvin E. Roth and Lloyd S. Shapley, 'for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design'.
Simulation in this video: 10 + 10 people, random rankings (fixed seed); askers' average partner rank 2.2 vs 4.8 for those waiting; with sides swapped 2.1 vs 4.4.
